title: A Prophet in the Mud Pit
overview: Jeremiah is thrown into a muddy pit for urging surrender to Babylon, is rescued by a foreign palace official, and then secretly tells a frightened king the same hard truth again.

parts.label: Thrown into the cistern (vv. 1-6)
parts.note: Jeremiah kept saying Babylon would take the city and that those who surrendered would survive, so four officials called this treason that was draining the soldiers' will to fight. King Zedekiah gave in to them, and they lowered Jeremiah into a drained water cistern, a deep underground storage tank, where he sank into the mud and was left to die.

parts.label: Ebed-Melek's rescue (vv. 7-13)
parts.note: Ebed-Melek, a palace official from Cush (a land south of Egypt), went publicly to the king and called the treatment wicked, and the king reversed himself and sent thirty men, probably enough to discourage the officials from interfering as well as to do the lifting. The small detail of padding the ropes with old rags shows real care for a weak, starving man.

parts.label: The king's secret question (vv. 14-18)
parts.note: Zedekiah met Jeremiah privately at a temple entrance and swore not to kill him or hand him over. Jeremiah's answer did not change: surrender to Babylon's officers and you, your family and the city survive; refuse and the city burns and you are captured.

parts.label: Fear and a mocking song (vv. 19-23)
parts.note: Zedekiah admitted he feared the Babylonians would hand him over to Judeans who had already defected, and that they would abuse him. Jeremiah warned that refusing would bring worse shame: the palace women would sing that his trusted advisers had led him into the mud and walked away, an image many readers connect with Jeremiah's own mud pit.

parts.label: A cover story (vv. 24-28)
parts.note: Still afraid of his own officials, the king gave Jeremiah a cover story, and Jeremiah used it, saying he had begged not to be sent back to the deadly prison cell in Jonathan's house, which was true but not the whole conversation. Readers have long debated how to judge that answer, and Jeremiah stayed under guard until Jerusalem fell.

think: What makes it hard to act on something you believe is true when the people around you are pushing the other way?
